Apple last month filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, accusing the company behind ChatGPT of stealing trade secrets related to hardware development. Nearly a month later, OpenAI has finally issued a detailed statement on its blog, addressing each of Apple's allegations one by one.

First, a brief recap of how events unfolded:

  • July 10: Apple filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging that a former Apple employee had systematically stolen Apple's trade secrets to help OpenAI develop its future hardware business.
  • July 10: OpenAI issued a brief response: "We have no interest in any other company's trade secrets, and we will continue to focus on developing innovative technologies that empower users around the world."
  • July 14: OpenAI updated its response, stating that it had not seen any evidence supporting Apple's allegations.

Subsequently, on the evening of August 4, OpenAI published a blog post providing a more detailed account of the incident. The full text is available here.

The post, titled "Apple is getting this wrong," is attributed to OpenAI.

OpenAI's latest response opens by characterising the lawsuit as "reckless, overly ambitious, and highly targeted":

OpenAI then appears to suggest that, prior to the lawsuit being filed, the company had not been formally notified of the issues at hand, including some of the details that were later reported:

They further publicly disclosed the contents of email correspondence, which can be viewed on that page.

Later, the response finally acknowledged some of the data access issues raised by Apple:

If you have read Apple's initial lawsuit filings, you would know that Tang Tan is one of the central figures in this complaint. OpenAI's response tonight defends him:

The remainder of the response consists of only two additional paragraphs of text, after which it transitions into screenshots of emails and iMessage conversations. Here is the final statement:

We wish Apple had communicated these concerns to us before filing, as we would have been happy to explain everything to them. We take the allegations in the lawsuit seriously and have expressed our willingness to work with Apple to resolve the matter. However, they have instead attempted to rewrite the narrative, including making vague allegations against other former employees, and will likely continue to do so. The basis for Apple's request for a preliminary injunction is built on misinformation and is entirely unnecessary, as we neither have nor want any of their trade secrets. What interests us far more is developing innovative products and technologies that push the frontier forward.

The above is the current state of affairs. This is not a legal response, but in the three and a half weeks since Apple initially filed, this is the most OpenAI has published (or shown).

A reminder that you can read OpenAI's latest response here, and revisit Apple's original complaint here.
